\chapter{Introduction and Project Vision}
\section{Project Overview}\label{ch1:sec:overview}
FlakeTrace is a self-hosted command-line tool that diagnoses \emph{order-dependent} test failures
in Java projects built with Maven and tested with JUnit~4 (including JUnit~3 test classes). An
order-dependent failure happens when a test passes on its own but fails after certain other tests
have run, because those tests left shared state behind.

The developer gives FlakeTrace the project folder and the name of the failing test. In
Iteration~1 this is one command:
\begin{center}
\texttt{py -m runner diagnose -{}-project <folder> -{}-victim <Class\#method>}
\end{center}
FlakeTrace then runs controlled test orders, each in a fresh JVM, and writes two files: an
execution record of every run, and a JSON report that follows the team's report schema
(Figure~\ref{ch5:fig:datamodel}). The report gives one of three outcomes:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{VERIFIED}: the tests responsible (the \emph{polluters}), a reduced order that
  reproduces the failure, how often it reproduced with a 95\% Wilson interval, and the shared
  resource with the exact code locations where it is written and read;
\item \texttt{CANDIDATE}: a reproducing order with a supporting resource, but a reproduction rate
  below the confidence threshold;
\item \texttt{UNRESOLVED}: no conclusion, with a typed reason such as \texttt{VICTIM\_FAILS\_ALONE}
  or \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED}.
\end{itemize}
FlakeTrace never changes the project it analyses: it reads the compiled classes, runs the tests
as they are, and hashes the project's files before and after every diagnosis to show this.

Its purpose is to replace the manual search developers do today, rerunning subsets of the suite
until the culprit appears, with a bounded diagnosis whose result anyone can check. It does not
detect flaky tests in general and does not repair them. Section~\ref{ch1:sec:scope} separates
what Iteration~1 has built from what is planned for FYP-2.
\section{Problem Statement}\label{ch1:sec:problem}
\begin{quote}
When a Java test passes in isolation but fails after other tests have run, developers can usually
detect that the instability exists but still have no bounded, reproducible, evidence-producing way
to identify which earlier test interaction caused it and decide what to inspect next.
\end{quote}
Stated precisely: a test suite runs in some order, and one test, the \emph{victim}, fails in that
order but passes when run alone. The problem is to find the smallest set of earlier tests, the
\emph{polluters}, whose running before the victim makes it fail; to show how reliably that reduced
order reproduces the same failure; to name the shared state that links the polluters to the
victim, at the exact places in the code where it is written and read; and, when the evidence does
not support an answer, to say so with a reason instead of guessing.

Three consequences follow from this statement and shape the whole project:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The input is a known failure.} FlakeTrace starts from a failing test the developer
  already has; finding flaky tests in the first place is not part of the problem.
\item \textbf{The output is evidence, not a fix.} The result tells the developer what to inspect;
  changing the code stays with the developer.
\item \textbf{The process is bounded.} An unbounded search is what developers already do by hand.
  Iteration~1 bounds the number of orders and repeats; an explicit execution budget is planned
  for FYP-2.
\end{itemize}
